was not fixed in respect of it or them; or
the end of that period if one was fixed.

This section has effect despite anything to the
contrary in any Act.

nodes.heading: Person may consent to imprisonment in respect of unpaid fines

nodes.text:
A person who has one or more warrants issued
against them under section 69, and who is already
in custody serving an uncompleted sentence of
imprisonment may request, in writing, the sheriff
to apply to the court for an order for that person to
serve a period of imprisonment in default of
payment of the outstanding fine or any instalment
under an instalment order under any one or more
warrants.

The Court may order that the person be
imprisoned in accordance with section 16(2) for a
term calculated in accordance with section 69N.

If the Court makes an order under subsection (2),
the Court may count the time served by the person
from the date the person requested the sheriff to
make an application under subsection (1) as time
already served for the purposes of the term of
imprisonment imposed on the person under
subsection (2).

A court may make an order under subsection (2)
whether or not the person is brought before the
court.

Subject to sections 16 and 18, a sentence of
imprisonment commences on the day that it is
imposed unless the offender is not then in custody
in which case it commences on the day he or she
is apprehended under a warrant to imprison issued
in respect of the sentence.

If an offender sentenced to a term of
imprisonment is allowed to be or to go at large for
any reason, the period between then and the day
on which he or she is taken into custody to
undergo the sentence does not count in calculating
the term to be served and service of the sentence
is suspended during that period.

If an offender lawfully imprisoned under a
sentence escapes or fails to return after an
authorised absence, the period between then and
the day on which he or she surrenders or is
apprehended does not count in calculating the
term to be served and service of the sentence is
suspended during that period.

Despite anything to the contrary in this or any
other Act or in any rule of law or practice, a
sentence of imprisonment must be calculated
exclusive of any time during which service of it is
suspended under subsection (2) or (3).

If an offender to whom subsection (3) applies is in
the period during which service of the sentence is
suspended under that subsection imprisoned or
detained in a youth justice centre or youth
residential centre under another sentence, the
unexpired portion of the suspended sentence takes
effect—

if it is to be served cumulatively on the
sentence or sentences he or she is then
undergoing—on the day that sentence is, or
those sentences are, completed; or

in any other case—at the end of the period of
suspension.

If an offender sentenced to a term of
imprisonment and allowed to be or to go at large
pending an appeal or the consideration of any
question of law reserved or case stated is
imprisoned or detained in a youth justice centre or
youth residential centre under another sentence at
the time when the appeal, question of law or case
stated is finally determined, the first-mentioned
sentence or the unexpired portion of it takes
effect—

if it is to be served cumulatively on the
sentence or sentences he or she is then
undergoing—on the day that sentence is, or
those sentences are, completed; or

in any other case—on the day on which the
appeal, question of law or case stated is
finally determined.

Subsection (6) applies unless the sentencing court
or the court determining the appeal, question of
law or case stated otherwise directs.

If a person serving a sentence of imprisonment
becomes a security patient, an involuntary patient
or a security resident, time spent as such counts in
calculating the term to be served.

nodes.heading: Time held in custody before trial etc. to be deducted from sentence12

history.raw: S. 18(1A) inserted by No. 10/1999 s. 18(2), repealed by No. 1/2000 s. 8(a), new s. 18(1A) inserted by No. 53/2003 s. 4(1), repealed by No. 30/2010 s. 7(a).
S. 18(1B) inserted by No. 10/1999 s. 18(2), repealed by No. 1/2000 s. 8(a).
S. 18(4A) inserted by No. 53/2003 s. 4(4), repealed by No. 30/2010 s. 7(a).
S. 18(5A) inserted by No. 53/2003 s. 4(5), repealed by No. 30/2010 s. 7(a).

nodes.text:
If an offender is in respect of an offence sentenced
to a term of imprisonment or to a period of
detention in an approved mental health service
under a hospital security order, any period during
which he or she was held in custody in relation
to—
must be reckoned as a period of imprisonment
or detention already served under the sentence
unless the sentencing court or the court fixing a
non-parole period in respect of the sentence
otherwise orders.
proceedings for the offence; or

proceedings arising from those proceedings
including any period pending the
determination of an appeal—

history.raw: S. 18(3)(b) amended by No. 6/2018 s. 68(Sch. 2 item 115.2).

nodes.text: Subsection (1) does not apply—

history.raw: S. 18(2)(ba) inserted by No. 48/1997 s. 11(2)(a), repealed by No. 65/2011 s. 9.
S. 18(2)(bb) inserted by No. 30/2010 s. 7(c), repealed by No. 48/2011 s. 15.
S. 18(2)(ca) inserted by No. 10/1999 s. 18(3), repealed by No. 1/2000 s. 8(b).

nodes.text:
to a period of custody of less than one day;
or

to a sentence of imprisonment or period of
detention in a designated mental health
service of less than one day; or

to a period of custody previously declared
under this section or section 35 as reckoned
to be a period of imprisonment or detention
already served under another sentence of
imprisonment or detention or Court Secure
Treatment Order imposed on the offender.

If an offender was held in custody in
circumstances to which subsection (1) applies,
then—

the informant or person who arrested the
offender must, if present before the court,
inform it, whether from his or her own
knowledge or from inquiries made by him or
her, of the length of the period of custody; or

if that person is not present before the court,
it may take and receive other evidence
(whether oral or written and whether on oath
or by affirmation or otherwise) of the length
of the period of custody.

If an offender was held in custody in
circumstances to which subsection (1) applies,
then the court must declare the period to be
reckoned as already served under the sentence and
cause to be noted in the records of the court the
fact that the declaration was made and its details.

The person with custody of the record referred to
in subsection (4) must indorse on the warrant or
other authority for the imprisonment or detention
of the offender particulars of the matters referred
to in that subsection.

If a person charged with a series of offences
committed on different occasions has been in
custody continuously since arrest, the period of
custody for the purposes of subsection (1) must be
reckoned from the time of his or her arrest even if
he or she is not convicted of the offence with
respect to which he or she was first arrested or of
other offences in the series.

If on an application under this subsection the
sentencing court is satisfied that the period
declared under subsection (4) was not correct it
may declare the correct period and amend the
sentence accordingly.

An application under subsection (7) may be made
by—
the offender; or

the Director of Public Prosecutions, if the
sentencing court was the Supreme Court or
the County Court; or

the informant or police prosecutor, if the
sentencing court was the Magistrates' Court.

history.raw: S. 18(2)(c) amended by No. 48/1997 s. 11(2)(b), repealed by No. 32/2013 s. 10(2).

nodes.heading: Subdivision (1A)—Indefinite sentences
nodes.text: Subdivision (1A)—Indefinite sentences

If a person (other than a young person) is
convicted by the Supreme Court or the County
Court of a serious offence, the court may sentence
him or her to an indefinite term of imprisonment.

A court must not fix a non-parole period in respect
of an indefinite sentence.

The court must specify in the order imposing an
indefinite sentence a nominal sentence of a period
equal in length to the non-parole period that it
would have fixed had the court sentenced the
offender to be imprisoned in respect of the serious
offence for a fixed term.

An offender serving an indefinite sentence is not
eligible to be released on parole.
A court may impose an indefinite sentence—
on its own initiative; or

on an application made by the Director of
Public Prosecutions.

A court may impose an indefinite sentence in
respect of a serious offence regardless of the
maximum penalty prescribed for the offence.

If a court is considering imposing an indefinite
sentence on an offender it must also consider
whether section 94B applies and, if it considers
that it does apply, the court must make a Court
Secure Treatment Order under section 94B.

nodes.heading: When court may impose indefinite sentence in respect of serious offence

nodes.text:
A court may only impose an indefinite sentence
on an offender in respect of a serious offence if it
is satisfied, to a high degree of probability, that
the offender is a serious danger to the community
because of—

his or her character, past history, age, health
or mental condition; and

the nature and gravity of the serious offence;
and
any special circumstances.

In determining whether the offender is a serious
danger to the community, the court must have
regard to—
and may have regard to anything else that it thinks
fit.

whether the nature of the serious offence is
exceptional;

anything relevant to this issue contained in
the certified transcript of any proceeding
against the offender in relation to a serious
offence;

any medical, psychiatric or other relevant
report received by it;

the need to protect members of the
community from the risk referred to in
paragraph (d)—

The prosecution has the onus of proving that an
offender is a serious danger to the community.

An application for an indefinite sentence by the
Director of Public Prosecutions—

may only be made if the Director has filed
with the court on the day of the conviction or
within 5 working days after that day a notice
of intention to make the application;

must be made within 10 working days after
the day of the conviction or within any
longer period fixed by the court during that
10 working day period.

On the filing of a notice under subsection (1)(a),
the court must revoke any order made for the
offender's release pending sentencing and remand
him or her in custody.

nodes.heading: Adjournment of sentencing
nodes.text:
If a court is considering imposing an indefinite
sentence on an offender, whether on its own
initiative or because of a notice filed under
section 18C(1)(a), it must on the day of the
conviction or within 5 working days after that day
explain, or cause to be explained, to the offender
in language likely to be readily understood by him
or her—
and adjourn sentencing until at least 25 working
days after the day of the conviction.

the fact that it is considering imposing an
indefinite sentence; and

the effect of an order for an indefinite
sentence—

history.raw: S. 18E inserted by No. 41/1993 s. 9, amended by Nos 24/1994 s. 6(1), 69/2005 ss 3(1)(c) (2)(3)(a), substituted by No. 26/2014 s. 433.

nodes.text:
If a court imposes an indefinite sentence on an
offender as mentioned in section 94(1)(b) after
considering the authorised psychiatrist's report
made after examining the offender subject to a
Inpatient Court Assessment Order made under
section 90, the court must deduct from the
nominal sentence the period of time that the
offender was detained under the Court
Assessment Order.

Section 94C applies if a person is found guilty of
a serious offence and a court imposes an indefinite
sentence in the same way it applies on any other
finding of guilt but as if—

section 94C(3) provided that the duration of
the Court Secure Treatment Order was for an
indefinite period; and

section 94C(4) did not require the fixing of a
non-parole period but instead required the
court to specify a nominal sentence as if the
Court Secure Treatment Order were an
indefinite sentence; and

in section 94C(5) the words "before the end
of the period specified in a Court Secure
Treatment Order" were omitted; and
section 94C(5) referred to—

an indefinite term instead of the
unexpired portion of the Court Secure
Treatment Order; and

release under a re-integration program
instead of release on parole.

A Court Secure Treatment Order made under
section 94B (as applied by subsection (2) of this
section) has effect for all purposes as an indefinite
sentence.

nodes.heading: Sentencing hearing
nodes.text:
Before imposing an indefinite sentence, a court
must—

give both the prosecution and the defence the
opportunity to lead admissible evidence on
any matter relevant to imposing such a
sentence;

subject to Division 1C of Part 3, take into
consideration any victim impact statement
made, or other evidence given, under that
Division;

history.raw: S. 18F(ab) inserted by No. 24/1994 s. 6(2), amended by No. 65/2011 s. 10(1).

nodes.text:
have regard to any submissions on sentence
made to it.

nodes.heading: Reasons for indefinite sentence
nodes.text:
A court that imposes an indefinite sentence on an
offender must, at the time of doing so—
state the reasons for its decision; and

cause those reasons to be entered in the
records of the court.

A court that imposes an indefinite sentence on an
offender must review the sentence—

on the application of the offender, at any
time after the expiry of three years from the
carrying out of the review under
paragraph (a) and thereafter at intervals of
not less than three years.

The Director of Public Prosecutions must make
the application to the court necessary for it to
carry out the review required by subsection (1)(a)
within the time specified in that subsection.

The court must cause a copy of an application by
an offender under subsection (1)(b) to be provided
to the Director of Public Prosecutions as soon as
practicable after it has been filed with the court.

Within 10 working days after the date of filing of
an application by an offender under
subsection (1)(b), the court must give directions
for its hearing and, subject to those directions,
must hear the application within 25 working days
after the date of filing.

A court on a review need not be constituted by the
same judge who constituted the court when it
imposed the sentence.

At any time after the making of an application
under section 18H(1)(a) or (b) the court may order
the Secretary to the Department of Health, the
Secretary to the Department of Human Services or
the Secretary or any other person or body to
prepare a report in respect of the offender and file
it with the court within the time directed by it.

The author of a report must conduct any
investigation that the author thinks appropriate or
that is directed by the court.

A report must relate to the period since the
indefinite sentence was imposed or last reviewed,
as the case requires.

The court must, a reasonable time before the
review is to take place, cause a copy of a report
ordered by it under section 18I(1) to be provided
to—
the Director of Public Prosecutions; and

the legal practitioners representing the
offender; and
if the court has so directed, the offender.

If the prosecution or the defence has caused a
report in respect of the offender to be prepared for
the purposes of the review, it must, a reasonable
time before the review is to take place, file it with
the court and provide a copy to the Director of
Public Prosecutions or the legal practitioners
representing the offender, as the case requires.

The Director of Public Prosecutions or the
offender may file with the court a notice of
intention to dispute the whole or any part of a
report provided under section 18J.

If a notice is filed under subsection (1) before the
review is to take place, the court must not take the
report or the part in dispute (as the case requires)
into consideration on the hearing of the review
unless the party that filed the notice has been
given the opportunity—
to lead evidence on the disputed matters; and

to cross-examine the author of the report on
its contents.

nodes.heading: Review hearing
nodes.text:
On the hearing of a review under
section 18H(1)(a) or (b), a court must—

have regard to any submissions on the
review made to it.

On a review under section 18H(1)(a) or (b) the
court, unless it is satisfied (to a high degree of
probability) that the offender is still a serious
danger to the community, must by order—
discharge the indefinite sentence; and

make the offender subject to a 5 year
re-integration program administered by the
Adult Parole Board and issue a warrant to
imprison in the same way as if it had
sentenced the offender to a term of
imprisonment for 5 years.

The indefinite sentence continues in force if the
court does not make an order under subsection (1).

nodes.heading: Re-integration program
nodes.text:
The provisions of Division 5 of Part 8 (parole) and
of section 112 (regulations) of the Corrections
Act 1986 apply to a re-integration program in the
same way that they apply to parole but as if—

references in those provisions to parole or
release on parole were references to a
re-integration program or release under a
re-integration program;

persons made subject to a re-integration
program were serving a prison sentence of
5 years during the whole of which they were
eligible to be released under the
re-integration program;

references in those provisions to a parole
order were references to an order made by
the Adult Parole Board releasing an offender
under a re-integration program;

references in those provisions to a
non-parole period were omitted;

references in those provisions to the parole
period were references to the period of
release under the re-integration program.

An offender may appeal to the Court of Appeal
against the refusal of a court to make an order
under section 18M(1).

The Director of Public Prosecutions may appeal to
the Court of Appeal against an order made under
section 18M(1).

On an appeal under this section the Court of
Appeal may—

in the case of an appeal under subsection (1),
confirm the refusal and dismiss the appeal or
uphold the appeal and make the order that it
thinks ought to have been made; or

in the case of an appeal under subsection (2),
confirm the order and dismiss the appeal or
uphold the appeal and set aside the order
made.

history.raw: S. 18O(3)(b) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 97(Sch. item 110.12).

nodes.text:
An indefinite sentence revives on the setting aside
of an order under section 18M(1) and the original
warrant to imprison or other authority for the
offender's imprisonment is to be regarded as again
in force.

history.raw: S. 18O(4) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 97(Sch. item 110.13).

nodes.heading: Offender to be present during hearings

nodes.text:
Subject to this section, the offender must be
present—

during the hearing of evidence under
section 18F;

during the hearing of a review under
section 18H(1)(a) or (b).

The court may order the officer in charge of the
prison or other institution in which the offender is
detained to cause the offender to be brought
before the court for a hearing referred to in
subsection (1).

Subsection (2) is additional to, and does not limit,
the court's powers under section 332 of the
Criminal Procedure Act 2009.

history.raw: S. 18P(3) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 97(Sch. item 110.14).

nodes.text:
If the offender acts in a way that makes the
hearing in the offender's presence impracticable,
the court may order that the offender be removed
and the hearing continue in his or her absence.

If the offender is unable to be present at a hearing
because of illness or for any other reason, the
court may proceed with the hearing in his or her
absence if it is satisfied that—

doing so will not prejudice the offender's
interests; and

the interests of justice require that the
hearing should proceed even in the absence
of the offender.

nodes.heading: Subdivision (1C)—Drug and alcohol treatment
nodes.text: Subdivision (1C)—Drug and alcohol treatment

nodes.heading: orders
nodes.text: orders

nodes.heading: Purposes of drug and alcohol treatment order

nodes.text:
The particular purposes of a drug and alcohol
treatment order are—

to facilitate the rehabilitation of the offender
by providing a judicially-supervised,
therapeutically-oriented, integrated drug or
alcohol treatment and supervision regime;

to take account of an offender's drug or
alcohol dependency;

to reduce the level of criminal activity
associated with drug or alcohol dependency;

to reduce the offender's health risks
associated with drug or alcohol dependency.

Nothing in subsection (1) affects the operation of
section 5(1) but, if considering making a drug and
alcohol treatment order, the Drug Court must
regard the rehabilitation of the offender and the
protection of the community from the offender
(achieved through the offender's rehabilitation) as
having greater importance than the other purposes
set out in section 5(1).

nodes.heading: Order only available at Drug Court
nodes.text:
Only the Drug Court may make a drug and
alcohol treatment order.

history.raw: S. 18Y inserted by No. 2/2002 s. 5, amended by No. 43/2020 s. 11.

nodes.heading: When drug and alcohol treatment order can be made

nodes.text:
The Drug Court may make a drug and alcohol
treatment order if—

an offender pleads guilty to an offence that is
within the jurisdiction of the Magistrates'
Court or the County Court (as the case
requires) and punishable on conviction by
imprisonment, other than—

a sexual offence as defined in
section 6B(1); or

subject to subsection (5), an offence
involving the infliction of actual bodily
harm; and

history.raw: S. 18Z(4)(a)(ii) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 97(Sch. item 110.19).

nodes.text:
the Drug Court convicts the offender of the
offence; and

the Drug Court is satisfied on the balance of
probabilities that—

history.raw: S. 18Z(2)(c) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 97(Sch. item 110.19).

nodes.text:
the offender is dependent on drugs or
alcohol; and

the offender's dependency contributed
to the commission of the offence; and

the Drug Court considers that, otherwise, it
would be appropriate to impose—

history.raw: S. 18Z(1)(d) amended by No. 65/2011 s. 13(1), substituted by No. 43/2020 s. 12(2)(c).

nodes.text:
if the proceeding is in the Magistrates'
Court, a sentence of imprisonment; or

if the proceeding is in the County
Court, a sentence of imprisonment of
no more than 4 years; and

the Drug Court considers that, had it been
appropriate to impose a sentence described
in paragraph (d), the Drug Court would not
have suspended that sentence in whole or in
part; and

the Drug Court has received a drug and
alcohol treatment order assessment report on
the offender under section 18ZQ.

The Drug Court Division of the Magistrates' Court
must not make a drug and alcohol treatment order
in respect of an offender who is subject to—
a parole order; or

a sentence of the County Court or Supreme
Court.

The Drug Court Division of the County Court
must not make a drug and alcohol treatment order
in respect of an offender who is subject to—
a parole order; or
a sentence of the Supreme Court.

The Drug Court Division of the County Court
must not make a drug and alcohol treatment order
in respect of an offender who is convicted of an
offence to which section 10, 10AA, 10AB, 10AC,
10AD or 10AE applies.

The Drug Court must not make a drug and alcohol
treatment order unless—

it is satisfied in all the circumstances that it is
appropriate to do so; and

the offender agrees in writing to the making
of the order and to comply with the treatment
and supervision part of the order.

Section 18ZC sets out what the treatment and supervision
part of the order is.

The Drug Court may make a drug and alcohol
treatment order in respect of an offender
regardless of whether—

the offender's drug or alcohol dependency
contributed on one or more previous
occasions to the offender—

failing to comply with the conditions of
bail or of a sentence; or

the offender has been previously sentenced
to one or more terms of imprisonment.

Despite subsection (1)(a)(ii), the Division of the
Magistrates' Court may make a drug and alcohol
treatment order in respect of an offender where
the offence involved the infliction of actual bodily
harm if it is satisfied that the harm was of a minor
nature.

A drug and alcohol treatment order may be made
in respect of one or more offences committed by
an offender.

An offender can only be subject to one drug and
alcohol treatment order at any particular time.

nodes.heading: Effect of Drug Court declining to make an order

history.raw: S. 18ZB inserted by No. 2/2002 s. 5, amended by No. 43/2020 s. 14(1)(3) (ILA s. 39B(1)).

nodes.text:
If an offender has pleaded guilty to an offence or
offences in respect of which the Drug Court could
make a drug and alcohol treatment order but it
does not consider it appropriate to do so, the Drug
Court must—

sentence the offender in relation to the
offence or offences if the offender consents
to the Drug Court doing so; or

adjourn the matter for sentencing in
accordance with subsection (2) or (3)
(whichever is applicable).

If the Drug Court Division of the Magistrates'
Court is to adjourn a matter under subsection

(b), it must adjourn the matter to the
Magistrates' Court (other than the Drug Court) at
the same venue.

If the Drug Court Division of the County Court is
to adjourn a matter under subsection (1)(b), it may
adjourn the matter to either—

if the offence is within the jurisdiction of the
Magistrates' Court, the Magistrates' Court; or

in any case, the County Court (other than the
Drug Court) at the same venue.

nodes.heading: The parts of a drug and alcohol treatment order

nodes.text:
A drug and alcohol treatment order consists of 2
parts—
the treatment and supervision part; and
the custodial part.

The custodial part of a drug and alcohol treatment
order consists of the sentence of imprisonment
that the Drug Court must impose on the offender
under section 18ZD.

The treatment and supervision part of a drug and
alcohol treatment order consists of—
the core conditions attached to the order; and
the program conditions attached to the order.
The core conditions operate—

if the custodial part is a sentence of
imprisonment of no more than 2 years—
for 2 years; or

if the treatment and supervision part is
cancelled earlier under section 18ZK,
18ZN or 18ZP, until that cancellation;
or

if the custodial part is a sentence of
imprisonment of more than 2 years—
for the length of the custodial part; or

if the treatment and supervision part is
cancelled earlier under section 18ZK,
18ZN or 18ZP, until that cancellation.
The program conditions operate—
for 2 years; or

if the treatment and supervision part is
cancelled earlier under section 18ZK, 18ZN
or 18ZP, until that cancellation.

The treatment and supervision part is taken to
continue to operate while either the core
conditions or the program conditions operate.

nodes.heading: Sentence of imprisonment must be imposed

nodes.text:
When making a drug and alcohol treatment order,
the Drug Court must impose on the offender a
sentence of imprisonment of no more than
the maximum duration specified in
subsection (1A).
The maximum duration is—

for the Drug Court Division of the
Magistrates' Court, 2 years; or

for the Drug Court Division of the County
Court, 4 years.

The Drug Court must impose the sentence of
imprisonment that it would have imposed if it had
not made the drug and alcohol treatment order.

Despite anything to the contrary in section 11, the
Drug Court must not fix a non-parole period in
accordance with that section as part of the
sentence imposed by it.

history.raw: Note to s. 18ZD(3) amended by No. 43/2020 s. 16(3)(b).

nodes.text:
A non-parole period may be fixed as part of certain orders
under this Subdivision activating the custodial part of a drug
and alcohol treatment order (see section 18ZE(3)).

nodes.heading: Activation of custodial part of an order

nodes.text:
Despite anything to the contrary in this Act, an
offender is not to serve the custodial part of a drug
and alcohol treatment order, and that part of the
order does not commence, except in accordance
with an order under this Subdivision activating
that part of the order.

The Drug Court may make an order activating some or all of
the custodial part under section 18ZL(1)(f) (which involves
serving a period in a secure custody facility), or under
section 18ZN or 18ZP.

In making an order under this Subdivision
activating some or all of the custodial part of a
drug and alcohol treatment order, the Drug Court
must first—

calculate the remaining length of the
custodial part of the order by subtracting
from the length of the sentence of
imprisonment imposed under the order—

each period of custody declared under
this Act as reckoned to be a period
already served under the sentence; and

each period of custody served in a
secure custody facility under the
custodial part of the order because of an
order under section 18ZL(1)(f); and
if required to do so by subsection (2A) or

, reduce the remaining length of the
custodial part of the order in accordance with
whichever of those subsections applies.

For the purposes of subsection (2)(b), if—
the remaining length of the custodial part must be
reduced so that the sum of those periods is
2 years.

the length of the custodial part of the drug
and alcohol treatment order is no more than
2 years; and

the sum of the following periods of time is
more than 2 years—

the remaining length of the custodial
part; and

the period during which the treatment
and supervision part of the order has
already operated—

For the purposes of subsection (2)(b), if—
the remaining length of the custodial part must be
reduced so that the sum of those periods is equal
to the length of the custodial part.

supervision part of the order operates, the

nodes.heading: Drug and alcohol treatment order assessment reports

history.raw: S. 18ZQ (2)(b)(i) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 97(Sch. item 110.21).

nodes.text:
If the Drug Court is considering making a drug
and alcohol treatment order at any stage after an
accused has indicated an intention to plead guilty
to an offence, or has pleaded guilty to an offence,
it must—

order a drug and alcohol treatment order
assessment report on the accused; and

adjourn the proceeding to enable the report
to be prepared by a specified Drug Court
officer.

history.raw: S. 18ZQ(7)(b) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 97(Sch. item 110.25).

nodes.text:
The purpose of a drug and alcohol treatment order
assessment report is—

to establish whether the accused is a suitable
person to be subject to a drug and alcohol
treatment order; and
if so—

to prepare a case management plan for
the accused; and

to establish whether the facilities
necessary to implement that plan exist
and, if so, to identify those facilities;
and

to make recommendations to the Drug
Court on the program conditions that
should be attached to a drug and
alcohol treatment order in respect of the
accused.

If the Drug Court grants an accused bail on an
adjournment under subsection (1) it must, for the
purpose of facilitating the preparation of the
report, impose a condition of bail requiring the
accused to—

history.raw: S. 18ZQ(3) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 97(Sch. item 110.22).

nodes.text:
report to the specified Drug Court officer, or
other specified person or body, within a
specified period; and

comply with any further reporting
requirements imposed by that officer, person
or body.

A drug and alcohol treatment order assessment
report may set out all or any of the following
matters which, on investigation, appear to the
specified Drug Court officer to be relevant to the
assessment of the accused and are readily
ascertainable by the officer—

history.raw: S. 18ZQ(4) substituted by No. 68/2009 s. 97(Sch. item 110.23), amended by No. 43/2020 s. 29(2).

the social history and background of the
accused;

the medical and psychiatric history of the
accused, including details of any treatment
the accused has undergone for drug or
alcohol dependency;

nodes.text: the educational background of the accused;
the employment history of the accused;

the circumstances of any other offences of
which the accused has been found guilty;
the extent to which the accused—

has complied with any sentence that is
no longer in force in respect of the
accused; and
the financial circumstances of the accused;
the housing history and needs of the accused;
any special needs of the accused;

any course, program, treatment, therapy or
other assistance that could be available to the
offender and from which he or she may
benefit.

The specified Drug Court officer must include in
the report any other matter relevant to the accused
which the Drug Court has directed to be set out in
the report.

history.raw: S. 18ZQ(5) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 97(Sch. item 110.24).

nodes.text:

later than the time directed by the Court.

Within a reasonable time after the report is filed
and before a drug and alcohol treatment order is
made, the specified Drug Court officer must
provide a copy of the report to—
the prosecutor; and
the legal practitioner of the accused; and

if the Drug Court directs the officer to do so,
the accused.

The prosecution or defence may file with the Drug
Court a notice of intention to dispute all or any
part of a drug and alcohol treatment order
assessment report.

If a notice is filed before a drug and alcohol
treatment order is made, the Drug Court must not
take the disputed report or disputed part of the
report into consideration when making the order
unless the party that filed the notice has been
given the opportunity—
to lead evidence on the disputed matters; and

to cross-examine the specified Drug Court
officer on its contents.

For the purposes of section 104ZY of the
Corrections Act 1986, a relevant person referred
to in that section who discloses to the specified
Drug Court officer information about the accused
for the purposes of the preparation of a drug and
alcohol treatment order assessment report is taken

or 257 of the Criminal Procedure Act 2009
against a sentence imposed by the Magistrates'
Court (including the Drug Court Division of the
Magistrates' Court), the County Court cannot itself

Act 2009 applies with respect to appeals to the
County Court against any sentence imposed by the
Drug Court Division of the Magistrates' Court

an appeal does not lie against—

drug and alcohol treatment order; or

drug and alcohol treatment order; or

the variation of the treatment and
supervision part of a drug and alcohol
treatment order; or

the drug and alcohol treatment order and not

reducing the length of the sentence of
imprisonment.

On the hearing of an appeal under section 254
or 257 of the Criminal Procedure Act 2009
against a sentence imposed by the Magistrates'
Court (other than the Drug Court Division of the
Magistrates' Court) at a particular venue of that
Court, if the County Court considers that the
making of a drug and alcohol treatment order may
be appropriate, it may refer the matter to the at
Drug Court Division of the Magistrates' Court that
or another venue for consideration of the making
of such an order, with or without any direction in
law.

However, if the offender has a usual place of
residence, the County Court may only refer a
matter under subsection (5) to the Drug Court
Division of the Magistrates' Court at a venue if the
offender's usual place of residence is within a
postcode area specified, in relation to that venue,
by the Minister by notice published in the
Government Gazette.

Despite anything to the contrary in the
Magistrates' Court Act 1989, a venue of the
Magistrates' Court to which a matter is referred
under subsection (5) is the proper venue of that
Court in relation to that matter for the purposes of
that Act.

If a matter is referred to the Drug Court Division
of the Magistrates' Court under subsection (5) but
the Drug Court Division of the Magistrates' Court
determines not to make a drug and alcohol
treatment order, the Drug Court Division of the
Magistrates' Court must remit the matter to the
County Court for the making of any order under
section 256(2)(a) or section 259(2)(a) of the
Criminal Procedure Act 2009 (as the case
requires) which the County Court can make.

If a matter is referred to the Drug Court Division
of the Magistrates' Court under subsection (5) and
the Drug Court Division of the Magistrates' Court
makes a drug and alcohol treatment order, the
order has effect for the purposes of Part 6.1 of
Chapter 6 of the Criminal Procedure Act 2009
as if it were a sentence imposed by the County
Court on the hearing of the appeal but for all other
purposes has effect as an order of the Drug Court
Division of the Magistrates' Court.

In this section, a reference to the County Court is
to be construed as a reference to the Court of
Appeal if the appeal is from the Magistrates' Court
or the Drug Court Division of the Magistrates'
Court constituted by the Chief Magistrate who is a
dual commission holder.

history.raw: S. 18ZR(10) inserted by No. 3/2016 s. 57, amended by Nos 43/2020 s. 30(10), 1/2022 s. 81.

nodes.heading: Immunity from prosecution for certain offences

nodes.text:
A person is not liable to prosecution for any
offence comprising the unlawful possession or use
of drugs of addiction—

as a result of any admission made in
connection with any assessment of the
eligibility of the person for the making of a
drug and alcohol treatment order; or

as a result of any admission made in
connection with the assessment by the Drug
Court, or at a case conference convened
under section 18ZI(1) by the judicial officer
constituting the Drug Court, of the person's
progress under a drug and alcohol treatment
order.

Subsection (1) does not prevent a prosecution for
any offence comprising the unlawful possession
or use of drugs of addiction if there is evidence,
other than the admission or evidence obtained as a
result of the admission, to support a charge.

The admission, and any evidence obtained as a
result of the admission, is not admissible against
the person in a prosecution referred to in
subsection (2).

In this section—
judicial officer means—

for the Drug Court Division of the
Magistrates' Court, a magistrate; or

for the Drug Court Division of the County
Court, a judicial registrar, an associate judge
or a judge of the County Court.

nodes.heading: Order made by Court of Appeal
nodes.text:
For the purposes of any proceeding under this
Subdivision—

history.raw: New s. 18ZT inserted by No. 26/2012 s. 29.

nodes.text:
a drug and alcohol treatment order made by
the Court of Appeal on an appeal must be
taken to have been made by the court from
whose decision the appeal was brought; and

the provisions about proceedings under this
Subdivision apply as if the court from which
the appeal was made were the sentencing
court.

nodes.heading: Subdivision (4)—Youth justice centre orders
nodes.text: Subdivision (4)—Youth justice centre orders

nodes.heading: and youth residential centre orders
nodes.text: and youth residential centre orders

nodes.heading: Youth justice centre or youth residential centre order14

history.raw: S. 32 (Heading) inserted by No. 48/2006 s. 42(Sch. item 32.5).

nodes.text:
Subject to subsections (2A), (2B), (2C) and (2D),
if a sentence involving confinement is justified in
respect of a young offender a court may make a
youth justice centre order or a youth residential
centre order if it has received a pre-sentence
report and—

it believes that the young offender is
particularly impressionable, immature or
likely to be subjected to undesirable
influences in an adult prison.

In determining whether to make a youth justice
centre order or a youth residential centre order, a
court must have regard to—
the nature of the offence; and

the age, character and past history of the
young offender.

A court must not make a youth justice centre order
in respect of a young offender who at the time of
being sentenced is under the age of 15 years.

history.raw: S. 32(2A) inserted by No. 48/1997 s. 16(3), amended by No. 48/2006 s. 42(Sch. item 32.6).

nodes.text:
A court must not make a youth residential centre
order in respect of a young offender who at the
time of being sentenced is aged 15 years or more.

history.raw: S. 32(2B) inserted by No. 48/1997 s. 17(4), amended by No. 45/2019 s. 50(3).

nodes.text:
If a young offender is to be sentenced for a
category A serious youth offence, a court must
not make a youth justice centre order or a youth
residential centre order in respect of the young
offender unless the court is satisfied that
exceptional circumstances exist.

If—
a court must not make a youth justice centre order
or a youth residential centre order in respect of the
young offender unless the court is satisfied that
exceptional circumstances exist.

a young offender is to be sentenced for a
category B serious youth offence; and

the young offender has previously been
convicted of another offence that is a
category A serious youth offence or a
category B serious youth offence—

The maximum period for which a court may direct
that a young offender be detained in a youth
justice centre or youth residential centre is—

if the court is the Magistrates' Court—
2 years; and

if the court is the County Court or the
Supreme Court—4 years.

Subsection (3) applies irrespective of how many
offences the young offender is convicted of in the
same proceeding.

If—
the subsequent sentence must be taken to be a
sentence that the young offender be detained after
the completion of the prior sentence for the period
then remaining until that maximum period is
reached.

a sentence of detention is imposed on a
young offender already under such a
sentence; and

the subsequent sentence is cumulative on the
prior sentence; and

the aggregate of the periods of the unexpired
portion of the prior sentence and the
subsequent sentence exceeds the relevant
maximum period set out in subsection (3)—

This section applies if a young offender is
convicted by a court of 2 or more offences
which—
are founded on the same facts; or

form, or are part of, a series of offences of
the same or a similar character.

The court may impose an aggregate sentence of
detention in respect of those offences in place of a
separate sentence of detention in respect of all or
any 2 or more of them.

The term of the aggregate sentence of detention
must not exceed the total effective period of
detention that could have been imposed in respect
of the offences in accordance with this Act if the
court had imposed a separate sentence of
detention in respect of each of them.

If the court proposes to impose an aggregate
sentence of detention it must, before doing so,
announce in open court, in language likely to be
readily understood by the young offender—

the decision to impose an aggregate sentence
and the reasons for doing so; and

the effect of the proposed aggregate
sentence.

If the court imposes an aggregate sentence of
detention in respect of 2 or more offences, the
court—

is not required to identify separate events
giving rise to specific charges; and
is not required to announce—

the sentences that would have been
imposed for each offence, had separate
sentences been imposed; or

whether those sentences would have
been imposed concurrently or
cumulatively.

To avoid doubt, an aggregate sentence of
detention may be imposed in respect of
convictions for offences that are the subject of
a rolled-up charge or a representative charge.

A representative charge is a charge in an indictment for an
offence that is representative of a number of offences of the
same type alleged to have been committed by the accused.
A rolled-up charge is a charge in an indictment that alleges
that the accused has committed more than one offence of the
same type between specified dates.

Nothing in this section affects the requirements of
section 6AAA (sentence discount for guilty plea).

nodes.heading: Sentences to be concurrent unless otherwise directed15

nodes.text:
Subject to subsection (1A), every term of
detention imposed on a young offender by a court
(except one imposed in default of payment of a
fine or sum of money) must, unless otherwise
directed by the court, be served concurrently with
any uncompleted sentence or sentences of
detention or imprisonment imposed on the young
offender, whether before or at the same time as
that term.

If one or more of the offences referred to in
subsection (1) is—
any period of detention imposed on the young
offender for that offence or those offences must be
served cumulatively with any uncompleted
sentence or sentences of detention in a youth
justice centre imposed on the young offender,
unless the Court, at the time of sentencing, states
that the sentences are concurrent and gives
reasons for its decision.

history.raw: S. 33(1A) inserted by No. 43/2017 s. 51(2), amended by No. 3/2018 s. 29.

nodes.text:
an offence of escape from a remand centre, a
youth residential centre or a youth justice
centre; or

an offence involving property damage to a
remand centre, a youth residential centre or a
youth justice centre—

Every term of detention imposed on a young
offender by a court in default of payment of a fine
or sum of money must, unless otherwise directed
by the court, be served—
whether that other sentence was, or those other
sentences were, imposed before or at the same
time as that term.

cumulatively on any uncompleted sentence
or sentences of detention or imprisonment
imposed on the young offender in default of
payment of a fine or sum of money; but

concurrently with any other uncompleted
sentence or sentences of detention or
imprisonment imposed on the young
offender—

A sentence of detention imposed on a young
offender which is to be served concurrently with a
sentence of imprisonment must be served as
imprisonment in a prison until the young offender
has served the sentence of imprisonment.

This section has effect despite anything to the
contrary in any Act.

Subject to sections 33 and 35, a sentence of
detention commences—

if the young offender is immediately
detained in custody under the sentence—
on the day that it is imposed; or

if the young offender is serving a sentence of
imprisonment which is cumulative on the
sentence of detention—on the day the
sentence of imprisonment is completed; or

in any other case—on the day the young
offender is apprehended under a warrant to
detain in a youth justice centre or a youth
residential centre issued in respect of the
sentence.

If a young offender sentenced to a term of
detention is allowed to be or to go at large for any
reason, the period between then and the day on
which he or she is taken into custody to undergo
the sentence does not count in calculating the term
to be served and service of the sentence is
suspended during that period.

If a young offender lawfully detained under a
sentence escapes or fails to return after an
authorised absence, the period between then and
the day on which he or she surrenders or is
apprehended does not count in calculating the
term to be served and service of the sentence is
suspended during that period.

Despite anything to the contrary in this or any
other Act or in any rule of law or practice, a
sentence of detention must be calculated exclusive
of any time during which service of it is
suspended under subsection (2) or (3).

If a young offender to whom subsection (3)
applies is in the period during which service of the
sentence is suspended under that subsection
detained or imprisoned under another sentence,
the unexpired portion of the suspended sentence
takes effect—

if it is to be served cumulatively on the
sentence or sentences he or she is then
undergoing—on the day that sentence is, or
those sentences are, completed; or

in any other case—at the end of the period of
suspension.

If a young offender sentenced to a term of
detention and allowed to be or to go at large
pending an appeal or the consideration of any
question of law reserved or case stated is detained
or imprisoned under another sentence at the time
when the appeal, question of law or case stated is
finally determined, the first-mentioned sentence or
the unexpired portion of it takes effect—

if it is to be served cumulatively on the
sentence or sentences he or she is then
undergoing—on the day that sentence is, or
those sentences are, completed; or

in any other case—on the day on which the
appeal, question of law or case stated is
finally determined.

Subsection (6) applies unless the sentencing court
or the court determining the appeal, question of
law or case stated otherwise directs.

nodes.heading: Time held in custody before trial etc. to be deducted from sentence17, 18

nodes.text:
If a young offender is sentenced to a term of
detention in respect of an offence, any period
during which he or she was held in custody in
relation to—
must be reckoned as a period of detention already
served under the sentence unless the sentencing
court or the court making the order otherwise
orders.

history.raw: S. 35(1) amended by No. 48/1997 ss 11(4), 16(4), 17(7), substituted by No. 82/2006 s. 3(3), amended by Nos 82/2006 s. 7(2), 65/2011 s. 19, substituted by No. 32/2013 s. 12.

nodes.text: proceedings for the offence; or

proceedings arising from those proceedings
including any period pending the
determination of an appeal—

history.raw: S. 35(3)(b) amended by No. 6/2018 s. 68(Sch. 2 item 115.2).

nodes.text: Subsection (1) does not apply—

to a period of custody of less than one day;
or

to a sentence of detention of less than one
day; or

to a period of custody previously declared
under this section or section 18 as reckoned
to be a period of detention or imprisonment
already served under another sentence of
detention or imprisonment or Court Secure
Treatment Order imposed on the offender.

If a young offender was held in custody in
circumstances to which subsection (1) applies,
then—

the informant or person who arrested the
young offender must, if present before the
court, inform it, whether from his or her own
knowledge or from inquiries made by him or
her, of the length of the period of custody; or

if that person is not present before the court,
it may take and receive other evidence
(whether oral or written and whether on oath
or by affirmation or otherwise) of the length
of the period of custody.

If a young offender was held in custody in
circumstances to which subsection (1) applies,
then the court must declare the period to be
reckoned as already served under the sentence and
cause to be noted in the records of the court the
fact that the declaration was made and its details.

The person with custody of the record referred to
in subsection (4) must indorse on the warrant or
other authority for the detention of the young
offender particulars of the matters referred to in
that subsection.

If a young offender charged with a series of
offences committed on different occasions has
been in custody continuously since arrest, the
period of custody for the purposes of
subsection (1) must be reckoned from the time of
his or her arrest even if he or she is not convicted
of the offence with respect to which he or she was
first arrested or of other offences in the series.

If on an application under this subsection the
sentencing court is satisfied that the period
declared under subsection (4) was not correct it
may declare the correct period and amend the
sentence accordingly.

An application under subsection (7) may be made
by—
the young offender; or

the Director of Public Prosecutions, if the
sentencing court was the Supreme Court or
the County Court; or

the informant or police prosecutor, if the
sentencing court was the Magistrates' Court.

history.raw: Pt 3A (Heading) renumbered as Pt 3D (Heading) by No. 65/2011 s. 44.
Pt 3A (Heading and ss 83B–83K) inserted by No. 65/2004 s. 3.
S. 36 amended by No. 48/1997 ss 18, 19(1), 28(1), substituted by No. 65/2011 s. 21, amended by No. 69/2014 s. 17 (ILA s. 39B(1)).

nodes.text:
The purpose of a community correction order is to
provide a community based sentence that may be
used for a wide range of offending behaviours
while having regard to and addressing the
circumstances of the offender.

Without limiting when a community correction
order may be imposed, it may be an appropriate
sentence where, before the ability of the court to
impose a suspended sentence was abolished, the
court may have imposed a sentence of
imprisonment and then suspended in whole that
sentence of imprisonment.

nodes.heading: Community correction order
nodes.text:
Subject to any specific provision relating to the
offence, a court may make a community
correction order in respect of an offender if—

history.raw: S. 37 amended by No. 19/1999 s. 8(1), substituted by No. 65/2011 s. 21, amended by No. 65/2016 s. 9.

nodes.text:
the offender has been convicted or found
guilty of an offence punishable by more than
5 penalty units; and

the court has received a pre-sentence report
(if required) and has had regard to any
recommendations, information or matters
identified in the report; and
the offender consents to the order.

nodes.heading: Period and commencement of a community correction order

history.raw: S. 38 amended by No. 48/1997 s. 28(2), substituted by No. 65/2011 s. 21.

nodes.text:
The period of a community correction order is the
period determined by the court which must not
exceed—

in the case of an order made by the
Magistrates' Court—
in respect of one offence, 2 years; or
in respect of 2 offences, 4 years; or

in respect of 3 or more offences,
5 years; or

in the case of an order made by the County
Court or the Supreme Court in respect of
one, or more than one, offence, 5 years.

Unless section 44(3) applies, a community
correction order must commence on a date
specified by the court that is not later than
3 months after the making of the order.

history.raw: S. 39 amended by No. 41/1993 s. 11, substituted by No. 65/2011 s. 21.

nodes.text:
If the court is making a community correction
order for a period of 6 months or longer, the court
may fix a period (being part of the period for
which the order is in force) as the intensive
compliance period.

Where a court is making a community correction order that
has a period of, for example, 2 years, the intensive
compliance period fixed by the court may be for a lesser
period of, for example, 8 months.

A court that fixes an intensive compliance period
under subsection (1) must determine that one or
more conditions attached to a community
correction order are to be completed within the
intensive compliance period.

If—
the intensive compliance periods are to run
cumulatively from the commencement of the first
order and then the balance of the periods of the
orders are to run cumulatively.

a court is sentencing an offender in respect
of two or more offences in the same
proceeding; and

the court makes separate community
correction orders in respect of any two or
more of the offences, the periods of which
are cumulative; and

the court fixes intensive compliance periods
for the orders that are cumulative—

nodes.heading: Community correction order may cover multiple offences

nodes.text:
If an offender is convicted or found guilty by a
court of two or more offences, which are founded
on the same facts or form or are part of a series of
offences of the same or a similar character, the
court may make one community correction order
in respect of those offences in place of separate
orders in respect of all or any two or more of
them.

A community correction order that is being made
in respect of more than one offence must not
exceed the maximum period for which a
community correction order may be made under
section 38.

If a court makes separate community correction
orders in respect of two or more offences
committed by an offender, the conditions of those
orders are concurrent unless the court otherwise
directs.

The conditions of a community correction order
made in respect of an offender are, unless the
court otherwise directs, concurrent with those of
any other community correction order in force in
respect of that offender.

nodes.heading: Maximum cumulative community correction orders
nodes.text:
A court must not impose on an offender in
respect of 2 or more offences separate community
correction orders with cumulative periods that are
to take effect in succession for a period that
exceeds in the whole 5 years.

history.raw: S. 41A inserted by No. 30/2010 s. 17, repealed by No. 48/2011 s. 21, new s. 41A inserted by No. 79/2014 s. 56, substituted by No. 65/2016 s. 11.

nodes.heading: Concurrent unpaid community work where there are several orders

history.raw: S. 42 substituted by Nos 65/2011 s. 21, 26/2012 s. 31.

nodes.text:
The number of hours of unpaid community work
required to be performed under a fines order
must, unless otherwise directed by the court, be
performed concurrently with any hours of unpaid
community work required to be performed under
any community correction order that is in force in
respect of the offender whether the community
correction order is made before or at the same
time as the fines order.

In this section, fines order means a fine
conversion order or fine default unpaid
community work order.

nodes.heading: Fine and a community correction order
nodes.text:
A court may impose on an offender a fine
authorised by law in addition to making a
community correction order.

nodes.heading: Imprisonment and a community correction order

history.raw: S. 44 amended by No. 45/1996 s. 18(Sch. 2 item 11.9), substituted by Nos 65/2011 s. 21, 45/2012 s. 8.

nodes.text:
Subject to any specific provision relating to the
offence, when sentencing an offender in respect of
one, or more than one, offence (other than an
offence to which clause 5 of Schedule 1 applies),
a court may make a community correction order
in addition to imposing a sentence of
imprisonment only if the sum of all the terms of
imprisonment to be served (after deduction of any
period of custody that under section 18 is
reckoned to be a period of imprisonment or
detention already served) is one year or less.

history.raw: S. 44(1) amended by No. 32/2013 s. 13(1), substituted by No. 69/2014 s. 18(1), amended by No. 65/2016 s. 12(1).

nodes.text:
Subject to any specific provision relating to the
offence, when sentencing an offender in respect of
one, or more than one, offence to which clause 5
of Schedule 1 applies, a court may make a
community correction order in addition to
imposing any sentence of imprisonment.

history.raw: S. 44(1A) inserted by No. 69/2014 s. 18(1), amended by No. 65/2016 s. 12(2).

nodes.text:
In sentencing an offender in accordance with
subsection (1) or (1A) in respect of 2 or more
offences, the Magistrates' Court must not impose
a sentence that exceeds in the whole 5 years.

history.raw: S. 44(1B) inserted by No. 79/2014 s. 57, substituted by No. 65/2016 s. 12(3).

nodes.text:
If a court makes a community correction order in
respect of an offender in addition to imposing a
sentence of imprisonment in accordance with
this section, the community correction order
commences on the release of the offender from
imprisonment.

A reference in this section to a sentence of
imprisonment does not include a sentence that has
been suspended.

If a court is sentencing an offender in respect of
an offence referred to in section 5(2GA) and the
court is satisfied under that subsection that an
order under this section is appropriate, the court
must make a community correction order with
the following mandatory conditions attached—
a judicial monitoring condition;
either—

a treatment and rehabilitation condition;
or
a justice plan condition.

This section does not limit the conditions which a
court may attach to a community correction order
made under this section.

Despite any other provision of this Part, a
condition referred to in subsection (1)(a) or (b)
must not be—

varied unless the condition as varied is
as onerous as, or more onerous than, the
previous condition; or
cancelled.

Section 43 does not apply to a community
correction order made under this section.
This section does not limit section 44.

history.raw: Pt 3 Div. 3 (Heading) repealed by No. 65/2011 s. 20.
Pt 3A Div. 3 (Heading) inserted by No. 65/2011 s. 21.
Pt 3C Div. 3 (Heading and ss 83AU– 83AZ) inserted by No. 65/2011 s. 60.

nodes.heading: Terms of a community correction order

history.raw: S. 45 amended by No. 45/1996 s. 18(Sch. 2 item 11.10), substituted by No. 65/2011 s. 21.

nodes.text:
The following terms are attached to each
community correction order—

the offender must not commit, whether in or
outside Victoria, during the period of the
order, an offence punishable by
imprisonment;

the offender must report to the community
corrections centre specified in the order
within 2 clear working days after the order
coming into force;

the offender must comply with any direction
given by the Secretary that is necessary for
the Secretary to give to ensure that the
offender complies with the order.

A direction may be given by the Secretary under
subsection (1)(f) either orally or in writing.

nodes.heading: Power of the Secretary to give written directions
nodes.text:
There is attached to each community correction
order the term that the offender must comply with
any written direction given by the Secretary for or
with respect to the following—

history.raw: S. 46 amended by No. 19/1999 s. 8(2), substituted by No. 65/2011 s. 21.

nodes.text: reporting to the Secretary; or
receiving visits from the Secretary; or

notifying the Secretary in writing of any
change of address or employment; or

obtaining permission from the Secretary
before leaving Victoria; or

if the order is subject to an unpaid
community work condition, performing
unpaid community work, including any
written direction as to the place, date or time
at which the work is to be performed; or

if the order is subject to a treatment and
rehabilitation condition, participating in a
treatment or rehabilitation program,
including any written direction as to the
place, date or time of the participation; or

if the order is subject to a treatment and
rehabilitation condition, undergoing any drug
or alcohol assessment or treatment, including
any written direction as to—

undergoing residential treatment or
assessment; or

the place, date or time that the
assessment or treatment must be
undergone; or

if the order is subject to a treatment and
rehabilitation condition, undergo any drug
or alcohol testing, including any written
direction as to the place, date or time that the
test must be undergone; or

if the order is subject to a treatment and
rehabilitation condition, undergoing any
medical assessment or mental health
assessment, including any written direction
as to the place, date or time that the test must
be undergone.

It is an offence under section 83AF for an offender to contravene a
written direction given by the Secretary.

A court that is making a community correction
order must attach at least one condition in
accordance with subsection (2).

A court that is making a community correction
order may—

attach one or more conditions under
Division 4; or

attach a condition under Division 2 of
Part 3BA.

A court that is making a community correction
order may attach in addition to a condition
attached in accordance with section 47 any other
condition to the order that the court thinks fit,
other than a condition about making restitution or
the payment of compensation, costs or damages.

A condition attached under subsection (1) to a
community correction order must not be about the
subject matter of a condition under Division 4 or
Division 2 of Part 3BA.

nodes.heading: Matters to be considered when attaching conditions
nodes.text:
The court must attach conditions to a community
correction order in accordance with—
the principle of proportionality; and

the purposes for which a sentence may be
imposed as set out in section 5; and

the purpose of a community correction order
set out in section 36.

history.raw: Pt 3A Div. 4 (Heading) inserted by No. 65/2011 s. 21.
Pt 4 Div. 4 (Heading and ss 89DC– 89DH) inserted by No. 15/2014 s. 7.

nodes.heading: Definitions
nodes.text: In this Division—

nodes.heading: child protection order
nodes.text:
means any of the following
orders under the Children, Youth and
Families Act 2005—

history.raw: S. 48B def. of child protection order inserted by No. 32/2013 s. 27(2), substituted by No. 61/2014 s. 170(2).

nodes.text: an interim accommodation order;
a family preservation order;

nodes.heading: family violence
nodes.text:
has the same meaning as in the
Family Violence Protection Act 2008;

nodes.heading: safety
nodes.text:
means safety from family violence,
physical or mental harm.

A court which is making a community correction
order may attach a condition requiring an offender
to perform unpaid community work.

The purpose for attaching an unpaid community
work condition is to adequately punish the
offender in the community.

Subject to section 48CA, the offender must
perform the number of hours of unpaid
community work specified by the court under an
unpaid community work condition.

If the Secretary gives a direction under
section 83AU the offender must perform the
number of hours of unpaid community work
specified by the Secretary.

The total number of hours for which an offender
may be required to perform unpaid community
work under an unpaid community work condition
must be determined by the court and must not
exceed 600 hours.

The total number of hours of unpaid community
work that the offender must perform in any 7 day
period must not exceed 20.

An offender may perform unpaid community
work for up to 40 hours in a period of 7 days if
he or she requests to do so and signs a written
consent to performing the extra number of hours.

If a court attaches an unpaid community work
condition as the sole condition under this Division
of a community correction order for up to a
maximum of 300 hours, the order expires on the
satisfactory completion of those hours of work.

If an offender is or will be subject to more than
one community correction order the court must
not make a direction under this Act that causes the
time limits that apply under all unpaid community
work conditions under the orders to exceed the
maximum time limits for the orders under
section 38.

When attaching an unpaid community work
condition the court may specify that the condition
applies for the period of the order or for any lesser
period specified in the order.

nodes.heading: Order with conditions under sections 48C and 48D

nodes.text:
This section applies if a court when making a
community correction order attaches both an
unpaid community work condition and a treatment
and rehabilitation condition to the order.

The court may determine that some or all of the
hours satisfactorily undertaken for treatment and
rehabilitation are to be counted as hours of unpaid
community work for the purposes of the unpaid
community work condition.

If a court makes a determination under
subsection (2) but does not specify the number of
hours undertaken for treatment and rehabilitation
that are to be counted as hours of unpaid
community work for the purposes of the unpaid
community work condition then all of the hours
satisfactorily undertaken for treatment and
rehabilitation are to be so counted as hours of
unpaid community work.

A court which is making a community correction
order may attach a condition to the order that
requires the offender to undergo treatment and
rehabilitation specified by the court and directed
by the Secretary unless otherwise directed by the
court.

When attaching a treatment and rehabilitation
condition the court must—

have regard to the need to address the
underlying causes of the offending;

have regard to the recommendations,
information and matters identified in the
pre-sentence report in relation to the
treatment and rehabilitation of the offender.

The treatment and rehabilitation that must be
specified by the court in a treatment and
rehabilitation condition must be any one or more
of the following—

any assessment and treatment (including
testing) for drug abuse or dependency;

any assessment and treatment (including
testing) for alcohol abuse or dependency;

any assessment and treatment (including
testing) at a residential facility for—

withdrawal from or rehabilitation for
alcohol abuse or dependency; or

withdrawal from or rehabilitation for
drug abuse or dependency;

any medical assessment and treatment that
may include general or specialist medical
treatment or treatment in a hospital or
residential facility;

any mental health assessment and treatment
that may include psychological,
neuropsychological, psychiatric or treatment
in a hospital or residential facility;

any program that addresses factors related to
his or her offending behaviour;

any other treatment and rehabilitation that
the court considers necessary and that is
specified in the order that may include
employment, educational, cultural and
personal development programs that are
consistent with the purpose of the treatment
and rehabilitation condition.

For the purposes of subsection (1) the Secretary
may give a direction to the offender—

to undergo the treatment and rehabilitation or
kind of treatment and rehabilitation specified
by the Secretary in the direction; and

in relation to any aspect of the treatment and
rehabilitation that the Secretary has
specified, a direction—

requiring the attendance of the offender
at a specified location; and

requiring the participation of the
offender in particular kinds of treatment
or rehabilitation.

A court which is making a community correction
order may attach a condition to the order that the
offender be supervised, monitored and managed
as directed by the Secretary.

The court may attach a supervision condition for
the purpose of addressing the need to ensure the
compliance of the offender with the order.

When attaching a supervision condition the court
must have regard to the information, matters and
recommendations made in the pre-sentence report.

When attaching a supervision condition the court
may specify that the condition applies for the
period of the order or for any lesser period
specified in the order.

A court which is making a community correction
order may attach a condition to the order directing
that—

the offender must not contact or associate
with a person specified in the order; or

An example of a direction that may be made under a
condition attached under paragraph (a) is that the
offender must not contact or associate with a
co-offender or co-offenders.

the offender must not contact or associate
with a class of person specified in the order.

An example of a direction that may be made under a
condition attached under paragraph (b) is that the
offender must not contact or associate with a member
of a specified club or association.

When attaching a non-association condition the
court may have regard to any effect the attaching
of the condition may have on any employment of
the offender.

When attaching a non-association condition the
court may specify that the condition applies for
the period of the order or for any lesser period
specified in the order.

A court which is making a community correction
order may attach a condition to the order,
directing that the offender must—
reside at a place specified in the order; or

An example of a direction that may be made under a
condition attached under paragraph (a) is that the
offender must reside at his or her current residential
address.
not reside at a place specified in the order.

An example of a direction that may be made under a
condition attached under paragraph (b) is that the
offender must not reside at the residence of a co-
offender.

When attaching a residence restriction or
exclusion condition the court may—

have regard to the risk the condition poses to
the safety of any person, including a child,
who is likely to reside with the offender
under the order; and

have regard to any effect the attaching of the
condition may have on any employment of
the offender.

When attaching a residence restriction or
exclusion condition the court may specify that the
condition applies for the period of the order or for
any lesser period specified in the order.

An offender to whom a residence restriction or
exclusion condition applies must not change his or
her place of residence unless the community
correction order to which the condition is attached
has been varied under section 48M(2)(d) to
specify the new place at which the offender must
or must not reside.

The court must not attach a residence restriction
or exclusion condition that is inconsistent with a
child protection order, a family violence
intervention order or a personal safety
intervention order.

A court which is making a community correction
order may attach a condition to the order,
directing that the offender must not enter or
remain in a specified place or area.

The following are examples of directions that may be made
under a condition attached under subsection (1)—

that the offender must not enter or remain in a specified
sporting venue in Victoria;

that the offender must not enter or remain in the central
business district of Melbourne.

Exclusion from a place or area that is a licensed premises
may be a condition of an order under section 48J, alcohol
exclusion condition.

When attaching a place or area exclusion
condition the court may have regard to any effect
the attaching of the condition may have on any
employment of the offender.

When attaching a place or area exclusion
condition the court may specify that the condition
applies for the period of the order or for any lesser
period specified in the order.

The court must not attach a place or area
exclusion condition that is inconsistent with a
child protection order, a family violence
intervention order or a personal safety
intervention order.

A court which is making a community correction
order may attach a condition to the order,
directing that the offender must remain at the
place specified in the order between specified
hours of each day for the period specified in the
order.

An example of a direction that may be made under a
condition attached under subsection (1) is a direction that
the offender must remain at home between 9pm and 6am
each day.

When attaching a curfew condition the court
may—

have regard to the risk the condition poses to
the safety of any person, including a child,
who is likely to reside with the offender
under the order;

have regard to any effect the attaching of the
condition may have on any employment of
the offender.

The offender must remain at a place specified by
the court under a curfew condition for—
for the period specified in the order which must
not be more than 6 months.
not less than 2 hours of each day; and
not more than 12 hours of each day—

If the Secretary gives a direction under
section 83AV the offender must remain at the
place specified by the court for the increased
hours or period that is specified by the Secretary.

The court must not attach a curfew condition that
is inconsistent with a child protection order, a
family violence intervention order or a personal
safety intervention order.

A court which is making a community correction
order may attach a condition directing that the
offender comply with the restrictions in
subsection (2).

For the purpose of subsection (1) and subject to
subsection (3) the restrictions are as follows—

the offender must not enter or remain in any
licensed premises characterised as a
nightclub, bar, restaurant, cafe, reception
centre or function centre; and

the offender must not enter or remain in the
location of any major event; and

the offender must not enter or remain in a bar
area of any licensed premises to which
paragraph (a) or (b) does not apply; and

the offender must not consume liquor in any
licensed premises to which paragraph (a)
or (b) does not apply.

When attaching an alcohol exclusion condition a
court may specify a licensed premises to which
the restrictions under subsection (2)(a), (b) or (c)
do not apply.

The court may attach an alcohol exclusion
condition to address the role of alcohol in the
offending behaviour.

When attaching an alcohol exclusion condition the
court may have regard to any effect the attaching
of the condition may have on any employment of
the offender.

When attaching an alcohol exclusion condition the
court may specify whether the condition applies to
the offender for a period of hours of each day or at
all times.

When attaching an alcohol exclusion condition the
court may specify that the condition applies for
the period of the order or for any lesser period
specified in the order.

history.raw: S. 48JA inserted by No. 65/2011 s. 58 (as amended by No. 26/2012 s. 71).

nodes.text:
A court which is making a community correction
order may attach a condition requiring an offender
to pay an amount of money as a bond, the whole
or part of which is subject to forfeiture if the
offender fails to comply with the order.

The court may attach a bond condition for the
purpose of ensuring the compliance of the
offender with the order.
When attaching a bond condition the court must—

have regard to adequacy of the financial
circumstances of the offender as contained in
the pre-sentence report to support the
payment of the bond; and

fix a time period for the payment of the bond
by the offender.

Any money paid by an offender under
subsection (1)—

must be paid to the court making the order;
and

despite any provision to the contrary in the
Supreme Court Act 1986, the County
Court Act 1958 or the Magistrates' Court
Act 1989, must be held on trust by the
Crown in a trust account established by the
Minister under section 23 of the Financial
Management Act 1994 until the money is
required to be repaid or forfeited under this
Act.

If any interest is received from the investment of
any money paid by an offender under
subsection (1) the interest must be credited to the
Consolidated Fund, whether or not any of the
money is repaid to the offender under this section.

If money paid under subsection (1) is to be repaid
to an offender as a result of the making of an order
to cancel or vary or otherwise deal with a
community correction order or bond condition
under section 48M(2) or 83AS(1), the Crown
must repay the money to the offender within
7 days after the order is made, unless the court
orders a longer period.

The Crown must repay to the offender any money
paid under subsection (1), that is not liable for
forfeiture under section 83AS(4) and that
subsection (6) does not apply to—
whichever is the later.
3 months after the expiry of the order; or

if no later than 3 months after the expiry of
the order, the offender is charged with an
offence punishable by imprisonment that was
committed during the period of the order,
7 days after the proceeding is finalised—

For the purposes of this section a proceeding is
finalised—

after the final determination of the charge by
a court; or
when the charge is withdrawn; or

when the prosecution of the charge is
discontinued.

All money forfeited to the Crown under
section 83AS(4) must be paid into the
Consolidated Fund.
